presEras.label: The Second Republic
presEras.blurb: The military handed power back in 1979 under an American-style presidential constitution: Shehu Shagari won the disputed 'twelve two-thirds' election, then a 1983 re-election so marred by rigging that the army seized power again within months.

presEras.label: The aborted Third Republic
presEras.blurb: Babangida's long transition produced the June 12, 1993 election — widely judged the freest Nigeria had held, won by MKO Abiola across regional and religious lines. The regime annulled it, Abiola died in detention, and the date became a national symbol; June 12 is now Democracy Day.

presEras.label: The Fourth Republic
presEras.blurb: Since 1999 Nigeria has elected its president seven times without the army returning — Africa's largest democracy by far. The era spans Obasanjo's two terms, the flawed 2007 handover, the 2015 election in which an incumbent conceded for the first time, and the three-way 2023 contest that Bola Tinubu won with just 36.6% of the vote.

legEras.label: The Legislative Council
legEras.blurb: Britain's 1922 Clifford Constitution created Africa's first elected colonial legislature — but only four seats were elected, by a few thousand propertied voters in Lagos and Calabar, while appointed officials held the majority. Herbert Macaulay's NNDP, and later Azikiwe's NCNC, built Nigerian party politics in this narrow arena.

legEras.label: Self-government and the First Republic
legEras.blurb: The federal elections of 1954 and 1959 divided the House along the lines of Nigeria's three regions — NPC north, NCNC east, Action Group west — and the 1959 contest chose the parliament that took the country to independence. The 1964 election, boycotted across the south amid census and alliance crises, broke the First Republic; the coup came thirteen months later.

legEras.label: The Second Republic
legEras.blurb: The 1979 constitution replaced Westminster with a presidential system and an elected National Assembly. The NPN dominated both chambers; the 1983 legislative elections, held in the same corrupted process as the presidential vote, were swept away with the republic that December.

legEras.label: The aborted Third Republic
legEras.blurb: Babangida's transition allowed exactly two parties — one 'a little to the left', one 'a little to the right', both written into existence by the regime. The 1992 Assembly it produced never mattered; Abacha's 1998 election, contested only by five parties that all endorsed him, was annulled when he died weeks later.

legEras.label: The Fourth Republic
legEras.blurb: The National Assembly elected since 1999 — 109 senators, 360 representatives — has been dominated by the PDP and, since 2015, the APC, but the 2023 election returned the most fragmented Assembly of the era, with eight parties winning Senate seats.

presidential.summary: Under the 1979 constitution, in order to be elected president on the first ballot a candidate needed to receive both the most votes nationwide and at least 25% of the vote in two-thirds of the states. However, at the time of the election, Nigeria had nineteen states, two-thirds of which in exact figures is 12.66.

presidential.caveat: Marred by massive rigging and violence; the army seized power within three months. Recorded here with that record.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Nigeria on 12 June 1993. The elections were the first held since the 1983 military coup d'état which ended the Second Nigerian Republic.
presidential.caveat: Widely judged the freest election Nigeria had held — and annulled by the Babangida regime before official results were declared. The figures here are the credible collated returns. Abiola never took office.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Nigeria on 27 February 1999. They were the first elections to be held since the 1993 military coup and were the first elections of the Fourth Nigerian Republic.
Presidential elections were held in Nigeria on 19 April 2003. The incumbent, Olusegun Obasanjo, was re-elected as the president of Nigeria.

Umaru Yar'Adua of the ruling People's Democratic Party (PDP) won the highly controversial presidential election, and was sworn in on 29 May. Election observers from the European Union described the elections as "the worst they had ever seen anywhere in the world", with "rampant vote rigging, violence, theft of ballot boxes and intimidation.".
presidential.caveat: Condemned by domestic and international observers as deeply flawed, with ballot-box stuffing and falsified returns; the winner himself acknowledged the process was defective.

presidential.summary: Presidential elections were held in Nigeria on 16 April 2011, postponed from 9 April 2011.

General elections were held in Nigeria on 28 and 29 March 2015, the fifth quadrennial election to be held since the end of military rule in 1999. Voters elected the President and members to the House of Representatives and the Senate.
General elections were held in Nigeria on 23 February 2019 to elect the President, Vice President, House of Representatives and the Senate.

General elections were held in Nigeria on 25 February 2023 to elect the president and vice president and members of the Senate and House of Representatives. Incumbent president Muhammadu Buhari was term-limited and could not seek re-election for a third term.

legislative.summary: Elective democracy had been introduced in Nigeria in May 1919, when the Townships Ordinance gave the right to vote for three members of Lagos Town Council to some men. The first elections to the council were held on 29 March 1920.
legislative.caveat: A Legislative Council election of the colonial era: only four seats (Lagos and Calabar) were elected, on a propertied male franchise of a few thousand, in a chamber dominated by appointed members.

legislative.summary: The 1922 Nigeria (Legislative Council) Order in Council provided for a 46-member Legislative Council, of which 23 were ex-officio officials, four were nominated officials, up to 15 were appointed unofficial members and four were elected (three in Lagos and one in Calabar).
legislative.caveat: A Legislative Council election of the colonial era: only four seats (Lagos and Calabar) were elected, on a propertied male franchise of a few thousand, in a chamber dominated by appointed members.

parties.name: National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons

legislative.summary: General elections were held in Nigeria between October and December 1954. The Northern People's Congress emerged as the largest party, winning 84 of the 184 seats.

parties.name: National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Nigeria on 12 December 1959. The result was a victory for the Northern People's Congress, which won 134 of the 312 seats in the House of Representatives, despite the National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons and Action Group receiving more votes.

legislative.knownAs: The election that broke the First Republic
legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Nigeria on 30 December 1964, although they were not held until 18 March 1965 in some constituencies in Eastern Region, Lagos, and Mid-Western Region due to a boycott in December.
legislative.caveat: Held amid the census and alliance crises and boycotted across much of the south; the disputed result helped destroy the First Republic.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Nigeria on 7 July 1979 for the first time since 1964 to elect a Senate and House of Representatives on 14 July. The result was a victory for the National Party of Nigeria, which won 36 of the 95 Senate seats and 168 of the 449 House seats.
Parliamentary elections were held in Nigeria in August 1983. The Senate was elected on 20 August and the House of Representatives on 27 August.
legislative.caveat: Held in the same corrupted process as the 1983 presidential vote.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Nigeria on 4 July 1992, the first time since the 1983 military coup. Only two parties were allowed to contest the elections, which resulted in a victory for the Social Democratic Party, which won 52 of the 91 Senate seats and 314 of the 593 House seats, despite the National Republican Convention receiving more votes.
legislative.caveat: Held under Babangida's military transition, with exactly two parties — both created by the regime — permitted to contest.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Nigeria on 25 April 1998. They were the first since 1992, following a coup in 1993.
legislative.caveat: Held under Abacha with five parties permitted, every one of which had endorsed him for president; annulled after his death weeks later.

legislative.summary: Parliamentary elections were held in Nigeria on 20 February 1999, following the annulling of the 1998 elections. The result was a victory for the People's Democratic Party, which won 59 of the 109 Senate seats and 206 of the 360 House seats.
